thoughts: अ is the independent letter for Hindi’s short, central vowel. The examples begin with the written letter अ and pronounce it.
description: Pronounce अ as a short “uh,” like the first sound in English “about.” Keep it brief, not like the long “ah” in “father.”

A familiar fruit

thoughts: आ is an independent vowel letter, usually found at the beginning of a word. After a consonant, the same vowel sound is written with ा instead.
description: A long, open “aa” sound, similar to the vowel in “father” for many English speakers. Keep it steady rather than turning it into a glide.

thoughts: इ is the independent vowel letter for the short i sound. The vowel sign ि represents the same sound when attached to a consonant and has its own guide.
description: Say the short i sound in English “sit,” not the long ee sound in “see.”

example_words.cultural_context: Steamed South Indian breakfast cakes

thoughts: ई is an independent vowel letter for a long ee sound. The examples show ई at the beginning of words, where this letter is used rather than the vowel sign ी.
description: Pronounce ई like the vowel in English “see.” Keep the vowel steady, without gliding into another sound.

thoughts: उ is the independent short-u vowel. These examples show it at the beginning of words, where it is pronounced like the vowel in English “book.”
description: Say the short vowel in “book” or “put,” not the longer “oo” in “food.”

example_words.cultural_context: Savory Indian breakfast dish
Language spoken in South Asia

thoughts: ऊ is the independent letter for Hindi’s long oo vowel. It usually appears at the beginning of a word; after a consonant, the same vowel is written with ू.
description: Pronounce ऊ like the vowel in English “food” or “moon.” Keep the sound steady, with rounded lips.

example_words.cultural_context: The material used to make sweaters
The word for energy or power

thoughts: In everyday Hindi, ऋ is usually pronounced like a quick “ri,” not like the syllabic r of Sanskrit.
description: Say a brief r followed by the short i sound in “bit”: roughly “ri.”

The Hindi word for a season
One of the ancient Vedas

thoughts: ए is an independent vowel letter. The examples use the letter ए itself, not the vowel sign े.
description: A steady ‘ay’ sound, similar to the vowel in English ‘day,’ but without the glide toward ‘y’ at the end.

example_words.cultural_context: The Hindi word for the number one
The familiar continent name
The heel of your foot

thoughts: ऐ is an independent vowel letter. In common Hindi pronunciation, it makes a long open-e sound; English speakers may be tempted to pronounce it like the vowel in “eye.”
description: Say a sustained vowel like the e in “bed,” with your mouth slightly more open. Do not glide into an “ee” sound.

thoughts: ओ is an independent vowel letter. It represents a steady /oː/ sound, unlike the vowel in many English pronunciations of “go,” which glides at the end.
description: Say the vowel in “go,” but keep your lips rounded and the sound steady rather than gliding toward “oo.”

example_words.cultural_context: Familiar sound and symbol associated with yoga and meditation

thoughts: औ is an independent vowel letter. In common Hindi pronunciation, it has an open, rounded vowel sound, without the strong glide of English “ow.”
description: Say a long “aw,” roughly like the vowel in English “saw.” Keep your lips rounded; avoid turning it into the “ow” sound in “cow.”

thoughts: ऑ is an independent vowel used chiefly in loanwords. The examples contain ऑ itself, not the related vowel mark ॉ.
description: Say a short, open ‘aw’ sound, like the vowel in ‘off’ for many English speakers. Keep it steady rather than gliding into an ‘oh’ sound.

example_words.cultural_context: A common three-wheeled taxi in India

The well-known film award

thoughts: ऍ is an uncommon independent vowel in Hindi, mainly used in some spellings of borrowed words. It represents a sound familiar to English speakers.
description: Say the short ‘e’ sound in English ‘bed’ or ‘apple.’ Keep it distinct from the longer vowel written ऐ.

example_words.cultural_context: The technology brand; this is an uncommon Hindi spelling of its name.

thoughts: अं combines a short vowel with a nasal sound. In these examples, the nasal sound changes to match the consonant that follows.
description: Say a short “uh,” then a nasal consonant. Before ग or क, the nasal sounds like “ng” in “sing”; before ड, it sounds closer to “n,” with the tongue curled back.

description: Say a short ‘uh’ sound, then release a soft breath like ‘h’: ‘uh-h.’ Don’t turn it into a strongly pronounced second syllable.

thoughts: क represents an unaspirated k sound. English speakers know the basic sound but may need to reduce the puff of air.

thoughts: This letter represents the ng sound English speakers use in “sing.” It is rare in ordinary Hindi spelling; familiar words often write the same nasal sound with ं instead.

thoughts: च is the unaspirated Hindi ch sound. English speakers know the basic sound, but may need to use less breath than in some English words.

example_words.cultural_context: The Hindi word behind the familiar drink chai

An everyday Hindi word meaning “truth”

thoughts: छ is the aspirated counterpart of च. English speakers know the basic “ch” sound, but may need practice making the following puff of air distinct.
description: Say the “ch” in “chair,” then release it with a strong puff of air. Hold your hand in front of your mouth to feel the puff.

thoughts: ज represents a familiar English consonant sound. Avoid examples where it is part of a longer combination taught separately.
description: Pronounce ज like the “j” in “jam.” It is voiced: you should feel your throat vibrate.

example_words.cultural_context: Popular spiral-shaped Indian sweet

thoughts: झ is the breathy, aspirated counterpart of ज. English speakers know the basic “j” sound but not usually this breathy version.
description: Start with the “j” in “jam,” then release it with an audible breath of air. It is not a separate “j” followed by an English “h.”

example_words.cultural_context: An everyday word for a lake

thoughts: As a standalone Hindi letter, ञ represents a palatal nasal. It is rare outside consonant combinations, which can have different pronunciations and are not examples of this sound on its own.
description: Make an “n” sound with the middle of your tongue raised toward the roof of your mouth, as in Spanish ñ. The letter on its own is pronounced roughly “nya.”

thoughts: ट represents a single unaspirated retroflex t sound. English speakers know a similar t, but may need practice with the tongue position.
description: Make a crisp ‘t’ sound with the tip of your tongue curled slightly back to touch the roof of your mouth. Unlike the t at the start of English ‘top,’ release it without a strong puff of air.

thoughts: ठ is an aspirated retroflex stop: English speakers may recognize the puff of air, but the tongue position is less familiar.
description: Say a strong, breathy “t” with your tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of your mouth. Release it with a noticeable puff of air. Unlike English “th,” it is not a continuous friction sound.

thoughts: ड represents a voiced retroflex stop. English speakers know the general d sound, but not usually this tongue position.
description: Like English “d,” but curl the tip of your tongue back to touch the roof of your mouth before releasing it. Keep your voice on and avoid a strong puff of air.

thoughts: ढ is a voiced, breathy retroflex consonant. It is distinct from ढ़, which has its own guide.
description: Curl your tongue tip back to touch the roof of your mouth, then release it with a voiced “d” sound and a noticeable puff of breath. English has no exact equivalent.

A common name for a casual Indian restaurant
Steamed savory snack from Gujarat

thoughts: ण is a retroflex nasal, distinct from the ordinary न. English speakers know the nasal sound but not usually this tongue position.
description: Say an “n” with the tip of your tongue curled back to touch the roof of your mouth, farther back than for an English n.

example_words.cultural_context: Name of the Hindu elephant-headed god

Everyday word for a school subject

thoughts: त represents an unaspirated dental t sound. English speakers know a similar sound, but its tongue placement takes practice.

A familiar style of Indian cooking
A central figure in the Ramayana

thoughts: थ is an aspirated dental stop, not the English “th” sound. The puff of air distinguishes it from त.

thoughts: द is a voiced, unaspirated dental consonant. English speakers know a similar sound, but need to move the tongue slightly forward.
description: Like the d in “day,” but touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your upper front teeth rather than the ridge behind them. Do not add a strong puff of air.

example_words.cultural_context: Familiar Indian lentil dish

A familiar nut

thoughts: ध is a voiced, breathy dental stop. The following examples show ध itself, not a separate consonant combination.

thoughts: न makes a familiar n sound, but the tongue touches the upper teeth rather than the ridge just behind them. The examples use न at the beginning or in the middle of a word.

thoughts: ब represents a familiar English-like b sound. Its pronunciation is distinct from the breathier भ.

example_words.cultural_context: A popular fragrant rice

thoughts: भ is a voiced, breathy version of ब. The examples show it at the beginning and in the middle of words.

thoughts: म makes the familiar English m sound. In these examples, it appears at the beginning or in the middle of a word.

thoughts: Hindi र is usually a quick tongue tap, unlike the sustained English r. These examples show र without the consonant clusters covered by separate guides.

thoughts: व is a single Hindi consonant whose pronunciation can range between English v and w. These are not usually separate sounds in Hindi.

thoughts: At the end of a word, ह is a light, voiced h-like sound. A final ह without a vowel mark usually has an inherent vowel before it, as in सुबह.
description: Pronounce a gentle, breathy h at the end. Unlike the h in English “hat,” your voice may continue vibrating as you say it. Don’t drop the final sound.

thoughts: At the end of a word, क़ represents a consonant without a following vowel. Many Hindi speakers pronounce it like क, though some preserve the deeper q sound.
description: Usually like the k at the end of “back.” In careful pronunciation, it can be a deeper sound made farther back in the mouth. Do not add a vowel after it.

description: Make a rough “kh” sound by pushing air across the back of your tongue, like the ch in Scottish “loch.” Unlike English k, you can hold this sound. Do not add a vowel after it.

description: Ideally, this is a soft, voiced friction sound made at the back of the mouth: keep air flowing where you would make an English hard “g,” rather than stopping it. In everyday Hindi, it often sounds simply like a final “g.” Do not add a vowel after it.

description: Curl your tongue tip slightly back and give the roof of your mouth one quick tap. It can resemble the quick ‘t’ in American English ‘butter,’ but the tongue is farther back. Do not add a vowel after it.

description: Curl your tongue tip back and flick it briefly against the roof of your mouth, adding a breathy release. It is not an English “d,” and there is no vowel after it.
